title: Thin places
hookLine: places where heaven and earth feel close

cards: A man on the run sleeps outdoors with a stone for a pillow. He dreams of a ladder set up on the earth, its top reaching to heaven, angels going up and down.
That's Jacob, in Genesis, fleeing his brother, a story first met on day three hundred sixty-two. When he wakes, he says: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not."
A bare patch of hillside had turned out to be a doorway. People who pray in the Celtic way have a name for spots like that. Today: thin places.

teach.h: WHERE HEAVEN AND EARTH FEEL CLOSE.
teach.b: A thin place, as people use the phrase, is somewhere the distance between heaven and earth seems to shrink, where the veil feels thin. Some name Iona, the small island off the west of Scotland linked with Saint Columba.
Others name a mountain, a shoreline, a ruined chapel, a back pew. This lesson won't claim an ancient source for the phrase itself. What's old is the experience.
Jacob's words go on: "How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." Dreadful, in the old sense: full of awe.

teach.h: THE GATE OF HEAVEN, AT A STONE.
teach.b: The gate of heaven, in a place with no temple, no altar, nothing but a stone. Jacob sets that stone up as a pillar, pours oil on it, and names the place Bethel. Here's a tension Christians hold.

Psalm one hundred thirty-nine asks where anyone could go to get away from God's presence, and its answer is nowhere. So why would some places feel thinner? One way Christians put it: it isn't that God is closer there.

teach.h: NOT GOD CLOSER: PEOPLE MORE AWAKE.
teach.b: It's that people are more awake there. Some places strip away the noise: wind, water, height, old stones, or a room where something true once happened. Jacob's own line holds both halves.
The Lord was in this place, and I knew it not. The thinness was on his side.

teach.h: A THIN PLACE NEEDN'T BE Well-known.
teach.b: So a thin place doesn't have to be well-known. A kitchen where someone you loved used to cook. A bench where someone heard hard news and somehow got through.
A small chapel in the middle of the night.

how: Some Christians make pilgrimages to places such as Iona, or keep a small local place, a chapel, a shore or a garden, where they go to pray; the idea of thin places is used in Celtic-style spirituality and retreat work.

games.q: you're Jacob. you've woken from a dream of a ladder to heaven, on a bare hillside, with a stone for a pillow. what do you do?
o: shrug it off and keep running.
set the stone up as a pillar, pour oil on it, and name the place.
games.why: Jacob sets up his stone pillow as a pillar, pours oil on it, and calls the place Bethel. the gate of heaven gets a marker.

practice: If there's a thin place near you, a window, a tree, a corner of a church, go there now or soon; if not, remember one, somewhere that seemed close to something more, and see it clearly: the light, the sounds, where you stood.
Don't explain it; just go back. If you pray, say Jacob's words: surely the LORD is in this place.

wordCard.voice: Thin places. Places where heaven and earth feel close, like Jacob's stone at Bethel: the gate of heaven, found on bare ground.

orig.note: Hebrew: Bethel, the name Jacob gives the place where he says this is none other but the house of God.

carryVoice: Your line: heaven is thin here. A bare hillside was a doorway all along. Rest well.
